name: Vocal fry and glottal control

lead: Vocal fry is the lowest vocal register, a slow, creaky sound made with loose glottal closure. Some people learn to control it so their voice sounds lower.

The vocal folds are slack and compressed and vibrate slowly and irregularly, giving the low rattle. Research covers how fry is produced and how listeners react. A 2014 study reported that speakers using fry were rated less competent, less trustworthy and less attractive, though that study has been criticised for using imitators. No trials test fry as an appearance method.

paras: People use it at the ends of sentences or as a deliberate low register, usually practised with recordings to hear how it comes across. It is generally used in small amounts rather than as a constant speaking style.
Occasional use is generally considered normal, but excessive use may signal a voice disorder or tire the voice. Listener studies report mixed social perceptions.

social.title: Creaky Voice: Another Example of Young Women's Linguistic Ingenuity
Creaky Voice: Yet Another Example of Young Women's Linguistic Ingenuity

angle.text: Some people use controlled vocal fry to drop the sound of their voice into a lower, creakier register. It works by loosening glottal closure so the folds vibrate slowly. Perception studies of creaky voice exist and are mixed; none test it for vocal attractiveness.

lead: Vocal fry, also called creaky voice or glottal fry, is the lowest vocal register, produced with loose glottal closure that yields a slow, popping or rattling sound at very low frequency.[1] In looksmaxxing voice discussion, some people try to control it to make their voice sound lower.

Researchers describe fry as a normal part of the pitch range that is not by itself a laryngeal pathology, though excessive use may signal a voice disorder.[1] Studies of listener perception are mixed in framing: one 2014 study reported that speakers using fry were rated less competent, less trustworthy and less attractive, though the study has been criticised for using imitators.[1]
No clinical studies were found that test fry as a method of appearance enhancement.

paras: In fry, the arytenoid cartilages draw together, compressing the vocal folds so they become slack and form a large, irregularly vibrating mass; well-controlled fry can extend far below modal voice.[1]

Fry has been linked to falling intonation in male Received Pronunciation speakers, and a 2010 study found increasing use among young American women. Other researchers reported women used it about four times as often as men when reading a passage in 2014.[1] In some languages, such as Finnish and Jalapa Mazatec, creaky voice has structural roles.[1]
Vocal pedagogues use fry to help singers with low notes who have excess laryngeal tension.[1]

Anderson and colleagues (2014) reported negative ratings for speakers using fry, with stronger reactions among female evaluators; linguist Rusty Barrett (2021) criticised the sample. Some commentators argue such judgments reflect broader policing of women's voices.[1]
No studies found testing fry or glottal control for appearance. Related research on listener perception and on fry in speech is summarised above.[1]
